proposal.original_claim_summary: The card treats Trump's January 20 Alaska resource executive order, later NPR-A leasing actions, ANWR changes, and the Ambler Road approval as one immediate opening of 16 million acres.

identified_problems.explanation: The January 20 order directed agencies to reverse prior restrictions; specific NPR-A, ANWR and Ambler actions occurred in later agency and presidential decisions across 2025.
The evidence reviewed does not support the stored claim that exactly 16 million acres were immediately unlocked on January 20.
The Ambler Road project was approved on October 6, 2025, not January 20.

proposed_split_entries.proposed_synopsis: Executive Order 14153 directed agencies to maximize Alaska resource development and reverse or review multiple Biden-era restrictions affecting ANWR, the National Petroleum Reserve-Alaska and other federal lands.

proposed_split_entries.proposed_synopsis: Interior released a draft analysis supporting a management alternative that would reopen up to 82% of the roughly 23-million-acre NPR-A to oil and gas leasing and development.
Trump approved AIDEA's appeal for the proposed 211-mile Ambler industrial road and directed agencies to issue the necessary authorizations.

frozen_original.title: Alaska Coastal Drilling Expanded; 16 Million Arctic Acres Unlocked
frozen_original.synopsis: On January 20, 2025, Trump signed an executive order rescinding Biden's 2024 memorandum protecting 16 million acres of Alaska's offshore and onshore territories from oil and gas leasing, including 2.8 million acres of the Beaufort Sea north of the National Petroleum Reserve. The order also revoked Biden's 2023 prohibition on drilling in major Alaskan coastal zones and directed the Bureau of Land Management to resume all leasing in the National Petroleum Reserve-Alaska. The administration additionally green-lit the Ambler Road project, a 211-mile road through ecologically sensitive Alaskan wilderness to access copper and cobalt deposits in a region with no existing road infrastructure.

proposal.original_claim_summary: The entry says Trump both declared a southern-border national emergency and invoked the Alien Enemies Act on January 20, 2025.

identified_problems.explanation: The border emergency and the Alien Enemies Act invocation were separate presidential actions almost two months apart.
Trump declared the border national emergency January 20, 2025, but invoked the Alien Enemies Act against Tren de Aragua on March 15, 2025.
The January 20 actions did not themselves invoke the Alien Enemies Act; they contemplated or prepared for further authorities.

frozen_original.title: Declares Border Emergency, Invokes Alien Enemies Act
frozen_original.synopsis: On January 20, 2025, Trump declared a national emergency at the southern border and officially invoked the Alien Enemies Act of 1798. This order initiated his long-promised mass deportation program, bypassing standard immigration courts. Civil rights organizations immediately filed lawsuits, warning the move was a catastrophic abuse of executive power aimed at militarizing immigration enforcement.

proposal.original_claim_summary: Trump allegedly said in April 2024 that he beat Barack Obama in the 2016 election and repeated the mistake.

identified_problems.explanation: No credible source matching the claimed April 2024 event was located; searches found distinct Obama/Biden or Obama/Clinton verbal errors at other dates.
The synopsis adds speculation about cognitive dysfunction, which should not be inferred from an unverified verbal error.

claims.claim: Trump repeatedly said at an April 2024 campaign event that he beat Barack Obama in 2016.

frozen_original.title: Trump Claims He Beat Barack Obama in 2016, Confusing Obama With Clinton
frozen_original.synopsis: At a campaign event, Trump stated he had beaten Barack Obama in the 2016 election, apparently confusing Obama — who was not on the ballot — with Hillary Clinton, who actually ran against him. Trump won the 2016 election against Clinton, not Obama, who was constitutionally ineligible to run for a third term. The error was not a slip of the tongue but was repeated in the same context. Cognitive health experts pointed to the confusion of well-known public figures in familiar contexts as a potential marker of cognitive dysfunction. The incident drew significant media scrutiny and comparisons to Biden's much-publicized gaffes, which Trump's camp had used as evidence of Biden's unfitness.

proposal.original_claim_summary: Trump Signs Executive Order Effectively Ending Independent Counsel Statute

identified_problems.explanation: The February 18 executive order 'Ensuring Accountability for All Agencies' chiefly concerns presidential supervision of executive and independent regulatory agencies and legal interpretations; it does not abolish the special-counsel regulations or an independent-counsel statute.
The federal independent counsel statute expired in 1999, so describing a 2025 order as ending that statute is inaccurate.

proposal.proposed_synopsis: Hide the current special-counsel/independent-counsel card. The closest February 18 order concerns presidential supervision of agencies and does not contain the claimed termination of special-counsel independence.

claims.claim: Executive Order 14215 expanded presidential supervision over executive and independent regulatory agencies.
The order ended an independent counsel statute or abolished special-counsel regulations.
claims.notes: The official order does not do so.

frozen_original.title: Trump Signs Executive Order Effectively Ending Independent Counsel Statute
frozen_original.synopsis: In February 2025, Trump signed an executive order asserting direct presidential supervisory authority over all Justice Department prosecutions and investigations — including those that had previously been designated as independent special counsel investigations — effectively ending the practical independence of any federal investigation that the President chose to override or terminate. The order claimed the Attorney General and all DOJ prosecutors served at the pleasure of the President and were subject to presidential direction in all matters. Legal scholars noted the order conflicted directly with the independent counsel regulations promulgated under federal law and with the constitutional principle that the executive branch cannot investigate itself. The order was seen as ensuring no independent special counsel could ever again investigate a president or his allies without the president's consent — the lesson Trump drew from his experience with Robert Mueller's investigation.

merged_description_snapshot.description_long: A former Justice Department civil-rights attorney accused Trump administration officials of deciding the outcomes of antisemitism investigations into Harvard and other universities before investigators had established whether civil-rights violations occurred. The whistleblower account said officials pursued sweeping penalties and included previously unreported details about a proposed settlement. The disclosure was shared with the House and Senate Judiciary Committees and later publicized by Representative Jamie Raskin. The allegations concern whether the administration’s response to antisemitism complaints was shaped by political pressure rather than evidence gathered by investigators. They do not establish that every alleged campus incident was false or that the whistleblower’s account has been adjudicated. Separately, a court restored nearly $3 billion in federal funding to Harvard, and the government appealed that ruling; the appeal remained pending in the First Circuit when The Harvard Crimson reported the disclosure. That funding dispute is related to the broader pressure campaign but is not itself proof of the whistleblower’s claim about predetermined findings. The account is an allegation from a former official and should remain attributed as such.
